687.title: Greater than our heart (1 John 3:19–24)
687.hook: when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart
687.howItsDone: Pastors and spiritual directors sometimes turn to 1 John 3:20 with people troubled by guilt or a harsh conscience, and some Christians memorize it as a comfort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in deed and in truth, and your line was not in word only. Which small deed did you do before saying anything about it? Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Some people have a prosecutor living in their head. It's a voice some people know well. It replays the awkward thing you said at the party. It reminds you of the mistake from ten years ago. It says, you call that love? After yesterday's passage, about loving in deed and in truth, that voice might be loud. Did I do enough? Have I ever really loved anyone that way? The writer of First John seems to know that his own words can set off the prosecutor. So right after asking for real, costly love, he turns to the reader whose heart is condemning them.

He says that by loving in deed we come to know we are of the truth, and "shall assure our hearts before him." Assure, here, means to calm, to persuade, to quiet down. Then the line: "For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things." Christians have heard this in two ways, and it's honest to say so. One reading hears comfort. Your heart is a harsh judge, but it isn't the final one. God is greater: he knows everything, including what you've forgotten, the good you did and the reasons you struggled, and, on this reading, merciful. Some older commentators heard a warning instead: if even your own heart condemns you, how much more does God, who knows all things? Both readings take God's knowledge seriously. Readers who favor comfort point to the paragraph's purpose, which is to settle the heart. Then the writer goes on: "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God." Confidence is a word for freedom of speech, being able to speak openly, like a child who isn't afraid to ask. And he sums up the whole commandment in a single sentence: "That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another." Believe and love. Two halves of one command. And at the end he names the way we know God lives in us: by the Spirit he has given us. In this letter, the heart is a witness, not the final judge.
screen: then, large: `GOD IS GREATER THAN OUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: quiet your self-accusing. Settle, and breathe. Let the prosecutor speak for a moment. What is it saying today? Hear it out, without arguing. Then imagine something bigger than that voice standing beside you. Not to shout it down. To know more than it knows. The context it forgot. The good it skipped. The reasons it ignored. Breathe in, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe out, and let the voice get quieter. If you pray, you can bring the accusation to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Confidence. First John's word for freedom of speech, speaking openly before God like a child unafraid to ask, when the heart does not condemn.
Your line: greater than your heart. Today, when the inner prosecutor starts up, say the line once in your head and then do the next good thing. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: Test the spirits (1 John 4:1–6)
688.hook: not every voice is from God; test it
688.howItsDone: Christians practice discernment by testing teachings against Scripture and the faith of the church, and some seek the help of a pastor, spiritual director or community; Ignatian discernment, from Ignatius of Loyola, is still taught today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart that condemns, and your line was greater than your heart. When the inner prosecutor started up, did you say the line? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Before there were labs, people tested gold by rubbing it on a dark stone and looking at the streak it left. Real gold left one color. Fakes left another. The stone was called a touchstone, and its lesson was simple: something can look exactly like gold and not be gold. Yesterday First John spoke gently to the heart that condemns itself. Now the writer turns brisk and practical: don't believe every voice. Test it.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world." Try, here, translates a Greek word that was also used for testing metal, an assayer's word. Notice he starts with beloved. This isn't a cynic talking. It's someone who loves his readers enough to want them not to be fooled. In his day, it seems, teachers were going around claiming the Spirit, and some of them said that Jesus didn't really come in a body. So the writer gives a test that fits his moment: "Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God." Remember the opening of the letter: what our hands have handled. The test is whether a teaching holds on to a real, touchable Jesus. Then a word of courage: "greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world." The reader isn't small and helpless before every persuasive voice. And then a sobering line: the world listens to its own. Popular doesn't mean true. Christians call this gift discernment. Paul lists the discerning of spirits among the Spirit's gifts. Over the centuries, churches have taught many ways to practice it. Catholic and Orthodox teaching weighs a claim against Scripture read with the church's tradition. Protestant teaching holds Scripture as the final test, often weighed with the counsel of a community. Ignatius of Loyola wrote rules for discerning the spirits that are still taught today. Each starts where the writer does: some voices sound like gold, and the letter says to test them before trusting them.
screen: `GREATER IS HE THAT IS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one claim before believing it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you heard or read this week that you accepted quickly. A headline, a rumor, a confident voice online, an inner voice that told you something about yourself. Hold it up like gold on a touchstone. Where did it come from? Who benefits if I believe it? Does it lead toward love, or away from it? Does it fit what I know to be true? Don't rush to a verdict. Just test it. If you pray, you can ask for discernment. The bell holds the time.
Discernment. The gift of testing voices before trusting them, the way a touchstone tells real gold from fake.
Your line: like gold on a touchstone. Today, before you share or repeat one thing, check where it came from. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: God is love (1 John 4:7–12)
689.hook: whoever loves is born of God, for God is love
689.carry: love, and do what you will
689.howItsDone: 1 John 4:7–12 is read at some Christian weddings and funerals, and some churches teach children 'God is love' as a first, short summary of the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word discernment, and your line was test the spirits. Which claim did you check before you shared it? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Church signs. Wedding programs. Bumper stickers. A pillow stitched in a grandmother's living room. The same three words turn up on all of them, printed so often they can start to sound like wallpaper. But they began in this letter, and they were not written as decoration. The writer has just told his readers to test every spirit, to watch out for voices that sound right and aren't. And then, right after that warning, he sets down the line all those signs borrowed. Today we hear those three words where they actually live.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God." Love comes from God, the way light comes from the sun. Then the reverse: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." Notice the order of those words. God is love. Not love is God. In the Greek the grammar makes that clear: God is the subject. The writer isn't saying that whatever we feel as love is divine. He's saying something about who God is: love belongs to God's very nature. So how do we know what that love looks like? He doesn't leave it abstract. "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." The love starts on God's side, not ours. Propitiation is a heavy word; it means the offering that makes things right between us and God. Christians explain how that works in different ways, but they agree on the direction: love reaching first. Then a startling line: "No man hath seen God at any time." Nobody. And yet, the next words: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us." In the writer's telling, the unseen God is found, in a sense, wherever people love. Centuries later, Augustine preached a series of sermons on this letter. In one of them he said, in Latin, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. He didn't mean anything goes. He meant that if love is the root within, what grows from it will be good.
screen: `GOD IS LOVE, NOT LOVE IS GOD.`
`HE LOVED US FIRST, AND SENT HIS SON.`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD. LOVE SHOWS HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone without conditions, starting here. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you love, but with a few conditions attached. If they'd only call more. If they'd stop that habit. If they'd say sorry first. Picture their face. Then, gently, set the conditions down, one at a time, as if you were taking stones out of your pockets. What's left when they're gone? Stay with that. Notice how it feels to love them as they are, this minute. If you pray, you can hold their name before God, just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Agape. Greek for self-giving love: First John's claim that God is love, not that love is God, and that love belongs to God's very nature.
Your line: love, and do what you will. Today, with the person you pictured, drop one condition for one whole day, and see what changes. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:13–18)
690.hook: there is no fear in love
690.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize 1 John 4:18 and pray it in times of anxiety, and pastors often use it to distinguish reverent awe of God from dread of punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three words, and your line was god is love. Which condition did you set down for a day? Day six hundred ninety.

Watch a toddler at the playground. They run off, climb something too high, look around, and find their parent's face. If the face is there, they go a little farther. If it isn't, panic. Psychologists have a name for this, a secure base: a child who's sure of being loved explores more, not less. Fear shrinks the world; love widens it. The writer of First John never read a psychology textbook. But he says something very close, in a single short verse about what love does to fear.

First he repeats yesterday's great line and adds to it. In the King James Bible: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Dwelleth means to live in, to stay, to make your home in. Love isn't only something God does; it's a place you can live. Then the verse: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love." Three things to notice. First, perfect doesn't mean flawless. The Greek word means complete, full-grown, mature. Grown-up love, not spotless love. Second, casteth out is a strong verb. It's the word for throwing something out the door. Love doesn't negotiate with fear. It shows it out. Third, fear hath torment. The word for torment can also mean punishment. The kind of fear he means is the dread of being punished, the fear of a child who expects to be hit. Here a fair question comes up. Doesn't the Bible also talk about the fear of the Lord? It does, often. Many Christian teachers have distinguished two kinds of fear. One is reverence, awe before something holy, like standing at the edge of the ocean. The other is dread, cringing before a punisher. The writer seems to mean the second. Reverence can stay. Dread is what love throws out. And the letter's context is judgment day: he says we can have boldness even then. Not because we're flawless, but because, as he says, as he is, so are we in this world.
screen: then, large: `THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let love answer one fear. Settle, and breathe. Name one fear that has been with you lately. Being found out. Being left. Getting it wrong. Getting sick. Say it plainly in your mind. Now ask it one question: what are you afraid will happen to me? Listen. Then, beside it, picture the face of someone who loves you, or, if you pray, the love of God. Don't argue with the fear. Just let love stand in the same room with it. Notice which one takes up more space after a minute. The bell holds the time.
Torment. The dread that perfect, full-grown love throws out the door, First John says, so that people need not live in fear of punishment.
Your line: no fear in love. Today, do one thing you've been avoiding out of fear, a call, a question, a no, and do it from love instead. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: We love because (1 John 4:19–21)
691.hook: we love him because he first loved us
691.howItsDone: 1 John 4:19 is a short verse some Christians memorize as a summary of their faith, and some churches teach it to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect love casts out fear, and your line was no fear in love. What did you do from love that fear had been holding back? Day six hundred ninety-one.

Stand at the edge of a canyon and say nothing, and the canyon says nothing back. Call out, and a moment later the rock answers in your own voice. An echo never goes first. It only exists because something reached it. Yesterday the letter said that love throws out fear. Today the writer asks where that love comes from in the first place. The passage is three verses long, and its first line is about exactly that: which love comes first, and which one answers.

In the King James Bible: "We love him, because he first loved us." Short enough to carry, and some readers hear the whole letter in it. In the writer's telling, our love is a response, and God's love goes first. Some readers also notice that the line still stands without the word him: we love, because he first loved us. Read that way, it isn't only, we love God because God loved us. It's, we love at all, anyone at all, because we were loved first. On that reading, every kind of love, for God and for neighbor, has the same source. Then the writer makes it very concrete, and very uncomfortable: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" He's not being harsh for the fun of it. He's pointing out something simple. God is invisible. Your brother is right in front of you, with all his irritating habits. If you can't love the one you can see, the claim to love the one you can't is hard to believe. It's a test anyone can turn on themselves, and the letter doesn't pretend anyone passes it cleanly. That may be why the test comes right after the line about who loved first. And then the last line of this section: "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also." One commandment, pointing two ways: up toward the God no one has seen, and sideways toward the brother in the next chair. The letter has been circling this from its first page. Light, children, deeds, fear. Here it lands: we love, because he first loved us.
screen: then, large: `BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive love before giving it. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to love anyone for a minute. Instead, remember being loved. A parent's voice. A friend who stayed. A teacher who believed you could. A stranger's kindness on a bad day. Let one memory come, and stay in it. Let yourself be on the receiving end, without hurrying to pay it back. Notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can receive God's love the same way, with nothing to do but be loved. Then, only at the end, notice whether anything in you wants to answer. The bell holds the time.
Echo. The hook's picture for our love: it never goes first, First John says, because he first loved us, and we only answer back.
Your line: he first loved us. Today, thank one person who loved you first, before you'd done anything to earn it. Day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: That you may know (1 John 5)
692.hook: the letter ends: little children, keep yourselves from idols
692.howItsDone: Some Christians read 1 John 5:13 as a word of assurance, and in teaching and preaching the letter's last line about idols is sometimes applied to anything, not only statues, that takes God's place in a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we love because, and your line was he first loved us. Did you let yourself receive some love before you gave any? Day six hundred ninety-two.

Some letters bury the point in the middle. This one saves it for the end. First John is a long, circling letter: light and darkness, love and fear, little children, test the spirits. Then, in the last chapter, the writer gives what some readers take as his reason for writing all of it. And he signs off with a line that seems to come out of nowhere. Not grace be with you. Not peace. Just this: little children, keep yourselves from idols. No explanation, and then amen. Today, the last chapter of First John: the reason for the whole letter, and its strange parting shot.

The chapter opens with how love works in practice. In the King James Bible: "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." Not grievous: not heavy, not a crushing load. And then: "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith." Then comes the purpose of the whole letter, in verse thirteen: "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life." That ye may know. Not hope, not guess, not lie awake wondering at night. Some readers hear the Greek verb here as settled knowing, the kind you don't have to keep checking. The letter has spent page after page on tests: do you walk in the light, do you love your brother. You might think the point was to make readers anxious. The writer says the opposite. He wrote so they could stop wondering and rest. One small note for anyone comparing Bibles. In the King James Bible, verse seven has a line about three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost. Some modern translations leave that line out or put it in a footnote, and their notes explain why. Churches that teach the Trinity draw it from many passages and the early creeds, not from this one verse. And then the ending: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Scholars aren't sure what he had in mind. Maybe the temple statues in a city like Ephesus, where tradition places the elder. Maybe the false pictures of God the letter has been warning about. Maybe anything that quietly takes God's place. The letter doesn't say. It just leaves the line ringing, like a parent calling after you at the door: take care of yourselves.
screen: `WRITTEN SO YOU CAN KNOW, NOT GUESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one idol, gently. Settle, and breathe. In the old sense, an idol is something carved and bowed to. In the wider sense some Christian teachers use, it's anything sitting in the center where something truer belongs. Your phone, maybe. Someone's approval. Money, a grudge, a plan for how life has to go. Let one come to mind. Don't scold it. Just name it, quietly, the way you'd name a houseguest who has stayed too long. Then let each breath move it one inch from the center. If you pray, you can rest on the old line from Psalm 46: be still, and know that I am God. The bell holds the time.
Idols. The strange parting shot that ends First John: keep yourselves from idols, after a letter written so its readers could know, not guess, that they have life.
Your line: keep yourselves from idols. Today, when a doubt or a worry shows up, notice it, and then go back to one thing you already know is true. Day six hundred ninety-two.

693.title: Face to face (2 and 3 John)
693.hook: two postcards from the elder: I'd rather not write with ink, but talk face to face
693.carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder
693.howItsDone: In Christian communities, hospitality and visiting, especially of the sick, the homebound and travelers, are a traditional part of life together, and 3 John's praise of Gaius is sometimes read as a picture of that welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of First John, and your line was that you may know. What idol did you name, gently? Day six hundred ninety-three.

Count the times this week you texted someone you could have called, or called someone you could have visited. No judgment; it's how a lot of life works now. Long ago, a church leader who calls himself simply the elder felt the pull the other way. Two of his notes survive in the Bible, Second and Third John, each only a page or so long. And both end with almost the same line: I have more to say, but I'd rather not say it in ink. I'd rather come and talk to you face to face.
screen: `I'D RATHER NOT WRITE IT IN INK.`

segments.voice: Second John is addressed "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth." Nobody knows who she is. She might be a woman who hosted a church in her home. Some readers think the elect lady is a way of naming a whole congregation, with her children as its members. The note repeats the heart of First John: love one another, walk in his commandments, and be careful of teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh. Third John is a note to one man, "the wellbeloved Gaius," and it reads like a personal letter. There's praise for Gaius, who opened his home to traveling teachers. There's a complaint about a man named Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence among them," and who turned those same travelers away. And there's a good word for someone called Demetrius. An old church quarrel, told in a few lines. Then both notes end the same way. In the King James Bible, Second John says: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full." The Greek is even more bodily than the English. It doesn't say face to face. It says mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma. Speak with your own mouth, close enough to hear the voice. The elder knew what ink can't carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder, the look on someone's face when they finally understand. And that closes this week. Greater than your heart. Test the spirits. God is love. No fear in love. He first loved us. That you may know. And now, face to face. A whole week about love, ending with an elder who would rather show up in person than write it down.
screen: `THE ELECT LADY: A WOMAN, OR A CHURCH?`
`A WEEK OF LOVE, ENDING IN PERSON.`
then, large: `THAT OUR JOY MAY BE FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit someone instead of messaging. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you mostly know through a screen these days: a grandparent, an old friend, a neighbor you only wave at. Picture their face. Not their profile picture: their actual face, the way it moves when they laugh. Then, in the quiet, choose one small way to be in the same room soon. A coffee, a walk, a knock on the door. If a visit isn't possible, a call where they can hear your voice counts. If you pray, you can hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Stoma. Greek for mouth: the elder's own word for face to face, mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma, the joy that ink can't carry and a visit can.
Your line: a tone, a hand on the shoulder. Today, swap one message for a voice or a visit, and notice one thing you'd have missed on a screen. Day six hundred ninety-three.
